title: Kaf
hook: kaf is a palm of the hand

segments.voice: Yesterday, the smallest letter, the yud that begins God's name and found its way into Joshua's. Your line was the smallest. What small thing did you do well? Today, a letter you can hold in your hand. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-nine.

Hold out one hand, palm up. Look at it for a second. It's the shape of asking, and the shape of offering. A beggar's hand looks like this, and so does a host's, saying come in, sit down. Now close it into a fist. Same hand, different message. Now just turn it over, palm down: covering, keeping, holding back. A hand can say a lot without a word. Hebrew has a word for the open, hollow part, the palm, the part that can hold water or hold out bread. Today's letter carries that word as its name.
screen: `PALM UP: ASKING, OFFERING.` → `A FIST.` → `PALM DOWN: HOLDING BACK.`

segments.voice: Kaf. The name of the letter is the word for the palm of the hand, and the Bible uses it in more than one place. Start with a bird. After the flood, Noah sends out a dove, and it comes back, because, in the King James, "the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot." In Hebrew, that sole is kaf too: the flat, open underside of a foot. So kaf is the part of you that meets the world. The palm that touches, the sole that stands. Next, a woman. The poem at the end of Proverbs, praising a woman of valor, says of her: "She stretcheth out her hand to the poor." The Hebrew there is kappah, her palm. She doesn't just give. She opens the flat of her hand. Some families sing that poem at the Friday night table. Then, a question at the gate. Psalm twenty-four asks who may go up into the hill of the LORD, and answers: "He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart." Clean hands, kapayim, palms again. Not only what the hand gives, but what it has held. Put the three together and kaf becomes a little map of a life: where you stand, what you offer, what you've touched. And there's a plain fact of the body here: a palm can't hold on and give at the same time. To hand something over, the fingers have to open first. Even before the hand gives anything, opening it is already half the gift.
screen: `THE SOLE OF THE DOVE'S FOOT.` · `HER PALM, OPEN TO THE POOR.` · `CLEAN HANDS, A PURE HEART.` · `STAND, OFFER, TOUCH.` · then, large: `OPEN THE FINGERS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open your palm. Settle, and rest your hands on your knees or in your lap. Close them gently into loose fists. Notice what you might be holding on to today: a worry, a grudge, a plan you're gripping too tightly. Then, slowly, turn your hands over and open them, palms up, fingers relaxed. Don't force anything out. Just let the hands be open. Breathe into the open space. If you pray, you can pray with your palms like this. The bell holds the time.
Kaf. The palm of the hand, the sole of the foot: the open, flat part that stands, touches and gives. Today's word.
Your line: open palm. Today, when you hand something to someone, coins, a cup, a pen, give it from an open palm and let go slowly. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Some families sing Eshet Chayil, the poem from the end of Proverbs that includes 'she stretcheth out her hand to the poor', at the Friday night Sabbath table; children learning the alef-bet may meet kaf as the palm of a hand.

fork.reveal: "the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot, and she returned unto him into the ark." the sole there is kaf.

original.note: Hebrew: palm of the hand, sole of the foot; also the name of the letter kaf (כ).

trapdoor: what you thought: kaf is the k sound.
what it means: the palm of the hand, open to give.
what a scholar hears: the same word is the sole of the dove's foot (Genesis 8:9), the palm stretched to the poor (Proverbs 31:20), and the clean hands of Psalm 24:4.

notes: All three verses quoted from the KJV (1769); a Keeper may prefer JPS 1917 wording.
Hebrew words: kaf raglah (Genesis 8:9), kappah (Proverbs 31:20), kapayim (Psalm 24:4). Confirm each is the kaf word in the Masoretic text.
'Some families sing' Eshet Chayil on Friday night; confirm phrasing. 'Woman of valor' is a common rendering of eshet chayil (KJV: 'virtuous woman'); not quoted.
The fork's reveal quotes Genesis 8:9 more fully than the teach; confirm.
howItsDone 'children ... often meet kaf as the palm': soft claim; Keeper may soften to 'may meet'.
